summary:
AEGIS: Crew Health Companion

On a mission to Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 20 minutes each way, so astronauts must notice and act on health changes themselves, without being doctors. AEGIS is a web app that helps them do that. It brings live NASA space weather (DONKI), real astronaut blood data (NASA OSDR, Inspiration4) and daily readings into one simple dashboard built around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. Each hazard has its own AI specialist agent, and the agents search a knowledge base of 202 NASA Human Research Program passages. A coordinator turns their findings into a calm briefing: what is happening, what to do now and what comes next, with every sentence citing NASA research. Astronauts can ask follow-up questions by text or voice. They can also take guided check-ins (including heart rate measured with the camera), explore a clickable body map, and follow a scripted emergency guide. Cited reports can be sent to the flight surgeon, with their arrival time shown. Simple rules, not AI, decide health status, and every number shows whether it is live, real or simulated. That keeps AEGIS transparent enough to trust when help is far away.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AEGIS is a crew health companion for long space missions. It helps astronauts understand their own health and act on it when Earth is minutes away.

The mission console shows one astronaut's health on a single screen, built from three datasets:

  • Live space weather from NASA DONKI: solar flares, particle events and solar storms.
  • Real astronaut blood tests from NASA's Open Science Data Repository: Inspiration4 studies OSD-569 and OSD-575, taken before launch and after return.
  • Daily readings such as sleep, mood, heart rate, blood pressure and cabin CO₂. These are simulated from published NASA figures and clearly labelled, or entered by the astronaut through guided check-ins.

AEGIS is built around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. Each hazard has its own AI specialist: the Space Radiation, Isolation & Confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity Fields, and Hostile & Closed Environments agents. Here is how a briefing is made:

  1. Simple, readable rules set each hazard's status (nominal, watch, alert or critical). When a signal changes, the relevant specialists are called in.
  2. Each specialist searches our knowledge base of 202 passages from NASA's Human Research Program, NASA podcasts and videos, and the Canadian Space Agency. The agents work in parallel.
  3. A coordinator merges their findings into one calm briefing: what is happening, what to do now, and what comes next.
  4. Every sentence must cite a NASA source. Anything without a valid source is removed before the astronaut sees it.

The astronaut can also:

  • Ask follow-up questions by text or voice. Answers stream in live, show each agent's work as it happens, and remember earlier conversations.
  • Take guided check-ins that explain how to measure and why it matters. Heart rate can be measured with the device camera.
  • Explore a clickable anatomical body map.
  • Follow a scripted emergency guide for chest pain, collapse or trouble breathing.
  • Send a cited report to the flight surgeon, with its arrival time shown given the communication delay.

What benefits does it have?

  • Astronauts don't have to be doctors. Numbers become plain-language guidance, with the reason behind each recommendation and a clear sign of when to involve the flight surgeon.
  • The crew can act during the communication delay instead of waiting up to 20 minutes for a reply from Earth.
  • Every claim can be checked. Each one links to the exact NASA passage it came from, and a "How this was made" view shows the signals, the agents, the passages read and the checks.
  • Data is labelled honestly. Every number shows whether it is live, real or simulated. The gap in in-flight blood samples is shown openly, not hidden.
  • Flight surgeons get compact, cited, time-stamped reports, so every message across the delay counts.

What is the intended impact?

AEGIS aims to make crews more autonomous and safer on missions to the Moon and Mars, where help is far away and resupply is rare. The same approach applies on Earth wherever people are far from a doctor: polar research stations, ships, remote and rural clinics. Guidance can be grounded in a trusted knowledge base and work when expert help is hours away. AEGIS also makes NASA's Human Research Program easier to explore: every hazard, risk and finding is one click away, with its original source.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and React Router, with live answers streamed through server-sent events.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI, with SQLite for conversations, memories, check-ins and reports.
  • AI reasoning: Claude Opus 5.5 through the Anthropic API, using structured outputs for the agents and streaming for chat.
    • NASA DONKI API;
    • NASA OSDR Inspiration4 datasets;
    • NASA Human Research Program pages, podcasts and videos (transcribed);
    • Canadian Space Agency pages.
  • On the device: camera-based heart rate (fingertip photoplethysmography) and the browser's speech recognition and speech synthesis.
  • Hosting: Render, for the API service and the static site.
  • Hardware: none beyond a laptop or phone. The camera stands in for a pulse sensor.
  • Design: custom vintage scientific illustrations created with generative image tools.

How is the project creative?

  • Organised the way NASA thinks about risk. Instead of a generic health chatbot, AEGIS gives each of NASA's five hazards its own specialist agent, coordinated into one voice.
  • Visible reasoning. The agents' work streams in live: which specialist was called, what it found and what it concluded. Every briefing can be traced back to its sources.
  • No new hardware needed. Heart rate is measured from the camera, so any device becomes a measurement tool.
  • A distinctive look. Vintage, scientific-plate illustrations and an engraved anatomical body map make the tool calm and memorable instead of clinical or sci-fi.
  • Communication delay is part of the design. It drives what the app recommends, how reports are timed, and when the crew should act on their own.
  • Realistic scenarios. A "landing day" scenario shows the gravity transition after months of weightlessness, and the real May 2024 solar storm can be replayed.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Safety and trust:
    • Fixed rules decide health status; the AI only explains.
    • Emergency steps are written in advance and never generated by AI.
    • Uncited claims are removed.
    • The app always says it gives guidance, not a diagnosis, and recommends the flight surgeon when needed.
  • Scientific honesty: we use real NASA data wherever it exists and label everything else as simulated.
  • Usability under stress: plain language, a dashboard that fits one screen, big buttons in emergencies, status never shown by color alone, voice input and read-aloud, plus day and night modes.
  • Privacy: the astronaut can see and delete everything AEGIS remembers, and the camera heart-rate video never leaves the device.
  • Different mission environments: the space station, a Moon base, a Mars base and deep-space transit, each with its own gravity, radiation dose rate and communication delay.
  • Practicality: runs in a browser, works on a laptop or phone, and deploys simply.
